title: Decks, Wheels and Bearings
bigQuestion: How do engineers choose the wood, urethane and steel in a skateboard, and what does each choice give up?

story.title: The Thumbnail Test
story.kicker: A shop worker uses one thumb to show why two wheels that look alike ride so differently.
paragraphs: A customer named Dani walks into a small skate shop with a cracked deck under one arm. She wants to build a new board for the concrete park across town. On the glass counter sit two sets of wheels. Both are white. Both are 54 millimeters across. To Dani they look exactly the same.

The shop worker, Marcus, picks up one wheel and presses his thumbnail hard into the riding surface. A small crescent-shaped dent appears and then slowly fades. He does the same to the second wheel. His nail barely marks it. "This one is 85A," he says, tapping the first. "This one is 99A. Same size, same color, very different ride."

He explains that the softer wheel squashes a little over cracks and pebbles. It grips the ground and smooths out the bumps on an old sidewalk. The harder wheel barely changes shape. On smooth park concrete it keeps more of its speed, and it slides when a skater wants it to. Dani realizes she has to decide where she will ride before she decides what to buy.

Then Marcus turns to the wall of decks. He flexes one between his hands and points to the stripes along its edge. "Seven layers of maple," he says. "Glued and pressed into this curve." He spins a wheel on a display truck, and it keeps turning for a long time. "And that is the bearings. Every part of this board is a choice somebody made."
story.think: If you could only buy one set of wheels for both a rough street and a smooth park, how would you decide on the hardness?

lessons.title: Seven Thin Layers of Maple
lessons.mainIdea: Most decks are seven thin plies of hard maple glued together and pressed in a mold, which makes them strong, light and springy.
reading: Look at the edge of almost any skateboard deck and you will see thin stripes. Each stripe is a *ply*, a sheet of wood usually under 2 millimeters thick. Most decks use seven plies of hard maple, a dense wood that grows in the northern United States and Canada. Stacked together, seven plies make a deck roughly 11 to 12 millimeters thick. That is thin enough to stay light and thick enough to survive landings.

The plies are not all laid the same way. Wood is strongest along its *grain*, the direction its fibers run. Most plies run with the grain along the board's length, which resists bending from nose to tail. One or more plies run across the board. These cross layers stop the deck from splitting along the grain when a wheel or tail strikes hard. Builders call this a *laminate*: thin layers glued so their strengths add up.

First, workers spread glue on each ply. Next, they stack the plies in order and set the stack in a mold shaped like the finished board. Then a hydraulic press squeezes the stack, and it stays under pressure while the glue sets. The mold gives the deck its upturned nose and tail and its curve from side to side. Finally, the pressed blank is cut to shape, drilled for the trucks, sanded and given a graphic.

Early boards from the 1960s were often a single plank of solid wood. A single plank can split along its grain and warp when it gets wet. Layered maple became the common choice because a laminate spreads stress across many glue lines. Some modern decks add layers of fiberglass, carbon fiber or bamboo, but seven-ply maple remains the most common recipe.

words.d: one thin sheet of wood in a layered deck; most decks have seven
the direction the wood's fibers run; wood is strongest along it
a material made of thin layers glued together so their strengths combine

look.title: Two Boards Side by Side
look.text: Picture two boards of the same size. One is a single plank of solid wood with all its grain running lengthwise. The other is seven thin plies, five running lengthwise and two running across. A skater lands hard and the back truck slams down near the tail. In the plank, the force pries along one line of fibers. In the laminate, the cross plies hold the lengthwise fibers together.
look.prompt: Which board is more likely to crack along its length, and which layer in the other board prevents it?

check.q: What is a ply in a skateboard deck?
choices: a metal plate under the trucks
one thin sheet of wood in the layered deck
check.why: A ply is one thin sheet of wood; most decks glue seven of them together.

check.q: Why do one or more plies run across the board instead of along it?
choices: to keep the deck from splitting along the grain
to make the wheels spin faster
check.why: Cross plies hold the lengthwise fibers together so a hard hit does not split the deck along the grain.

check.q: Which step comes right after the glued plies are stacked?
choices: the stack is pressed in a mold while the glue sets
the deck is cut to its final shape
check.why: The stacked plies go into a mold in a press; cutting, drilling and graphics come after the glue sets.

lessons.title: Concave and Stiffness
lessons.mainIdea: Bending a deck into a side-to-side curve called concave makes it much stiffer and gives the feet edges to press against.
reading: Hold a metal tape measure flat and push it out from the case. It droops after a short distance. Now let it curl into its normal curved shape. It can stick straight out much farther. The metal did not change. Only its cross-section, the shape you would see if you sliced it across, changed. A skateboard deck uses the same trick.

*Concave* is the gentle side-to-side curve pressed into a deck, with the edges higher than the middle. Engineers describe a shape's resistance to bending with the *second moment of area*. The farther material sits from the bending line through the middle of the cross-section, the larger this number and the stiffer the part. Curving the deck moves its edges up and away from that line. The same seven plies become stiffer without adding any weight.

Concave also helps the feet. The raised edges, called rails, give the toes and heels something to press and catch. When a skater flicks off the toe-side edge for a kickflip, the curve guides where the foot leaves the board. Steep concave locks the feet in place. Mellow concave feels flatter and more open, and some skaters find it easier to stand on for long rides.

Stiffness also grows quickly with thickness. For a flat strip, stiffness rises with the cube of its thickness. A deck that is 10 percent thicker is about 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.33 times as stiff, a third stiffer. It is also about 10 percent heavier. Concave lets a maker gain stiffness without paying that weight cost.

words.d: the side-to-side curve in a deck, with the edges higher than the middle
a number engineers use for how a cross-section's shape resists bending; material far from the middle raises it
the long side edges of a deck

look.title: Thickness and Stiffness
look.unit: times as stiff as a 10 mm deck
look.cite: Worked example: stiffness of a flat strip grows with thickness cubed (same width and wood)
look.prompt: Going from 10 mm to 12 mm adds 20 percent more wood. About how much stiffer does the deck get?

check.q: What does concave do to a deck's stiffness?
choices: it has no effect on stiffness
it only makes the deck heavier
it makes the deck stiffer without adding weight
check.why: Curving the cross-section moves wood away from the middle line, raising the second moment of area and the stiffness.

check.q: A flat strip is made 10 percent thicker. About how much stiffer does it get?
check.why: Stiffness grows with thickness cubed: 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.33, about a third stiffer.

check.q: Why does a curled tape measure stick out farther than a flat one?
choices: the metal becomes harder when curled
check.why: The metal is the same; its curved shape places material away from the bending line, so it resists bending.

lessons.title: Nose, Tail and Wheelbase
lessons.mainIdea: The kicked-up tail and nose make levers for tricks, and the wheelbase sets how stable or quick a board feels.
reading: Larry Stevenson of Makaha received a patent for the *kicktail* in 1971. A kicktail is the upturned end of a deck. Pressing it lifts the front wheels like a seesaw, so a skater can turn sharply or pop the board into the air. Modern decks have a kick at both ends. The two ends are often shaped a little differently so a skater can tell the nose from the tail without looking.

The tail works as a lever. The back truck's axle is the pivot. When the back foot pushes down on the tail, the rest of the board swings up around that axle. A longer, steeper tail gives the foot more distance from the pivot and lets it strike the ground sooner. A short, flat tail needs a bigger stomp to get the same lift.

The *wheelbase* is the distance between the two trucks, usually measured between the inner mounting holes. A longer wheelbase spreads the wheels apart. The board feels steadier at speed and turns in wider arcs. A shorter wheelbase makes quick turns and spins easier but feels twitchier going fast. Many street decks have a wheelbase of about 35 to 37 centimeters, and longboards stretch much longer.

Width matters too. Many street and park decks today are about 20 to 22 centimeters wide. A wider deck gives bigger feet more room and more stability on landings. A narrower deck is lighter and easier to flip. A skater with large shoes on a narrow deck may catch the toes or heels on tricks. The best width is the one that fits the rider's feet and style.

words.d: the upturned end of a deck that lets a skater lift the wheels; Larry Stevenson's patent was granted in 1971
the distance between the front and back trucks
the point a lever turns around; for an ollie, the back axle

look.title: The Tail as a Lever
look.text: Picture the board from the side. The back wheels sit on the ground. The back foot is on the tail, behind the back axle. The front foot is near the front bolts. When the back foot presses down, the tail drops and the nose rises, turning around the back axle like a seesaw on its center post.
look.prompt: If the back foot moves farther out onto the end of the tail, does it get more or less leverage, and why?

check.q: In 1971, who received a patent for the kicktail?
check.why: Larry Stevenson of Makaha received the kicktail patent in 1971.

check.q: When the back foot presses the tail, what does the board pivot around?
check.why: The back axle is the pivot; the tail goes down and the nose rises around it.

check.q: What does a longer wheelbase usually give a board?
choices: more stability at speed and wider turns
check.why: Spreading the trucks apart makes a board steadier at speed but turns it in wider arcs.

lessons.title: Measuring Wheel Hardness
lessons.mainIdea: Wheel hardness is measured on the durometer A scale, from about 78A for soft wheels to about 101A for hard ones.
reading: A *durometer* is a small gauge that measures how hard a material is. It presses a spring-loaded pin, called an indenter, into the surface. A soft material lets the pin sink in, so the gauge reads low. A hard material pushes back, so the gauge reads high. Skate wheels are rated on the Shore A scale, written as a number followed by A, such as 85A.

Skate wheels run from about 78A to about 101A. Wheels around 78A to 87A are soft. They feel cushy, grip well and roll quietly over rough pavement. Wheels around 88A to 95A are in the middle. Wheels around 96A to 101A are hard. They are built for smooth skatepark concrete, wood ramps and street spots with smooth ground. The scale is not a straight line of feel, so a few points near the hard end can feel like a big change.

The A scale tops out at 100, and readings near the top are less precise. For that reason some wheel makers rate very hard wheels on a B scale. The B scale uses a different indenter and reads about 20 points lower than A for the same wheel. An 83B wheel is roughly a 103A wheel. If two labels use different letters, the numbers cannot be compared directly.

Marcus's thumbnail trick from the shop is a rough version of a durometer. The softer wheel let his nail sink in and then slowly recovered. The harder wheel barely took a mark. A real gauge removes the guesswork by using the same pin and the same spring every time.

words.d: a gauge that measures hardness by pressing a spring-loaded pin into a material
the hardness scale used for most skate wheels, written like 85A or 99A
the pin in a durometer that presses into the material

look.title: Typical Wheel Hardness by Use
look.cite: Typical ranges sold for skate wheels; examples, not fixed rules
look.prompt: A skater rides only on cracked sidewalks. Which end of this chart should they look at, and why?

check.q: How does a durometer measure hardness?
choices: by pressing a spring-loaded pin into the surface
by spinning the wheel and timing it
check.why: A durometer presses a spring-loaded indenter into the material; a harder material resists more and reads higher.

check.q: Which wheel is softest?
check.why: On the A scale, lower numbers are softer, so 78A is the softest of these.

check.q: Why can't you directly compare an 83B wheel with an 83A wheel?
choices: B scale is only for bearings
the B scale reads about 20 points lower than A for the same wheel
the letters only show the color
check.why: The B scale uses a different indenter and reads about 20 points lower, so 83B is roughly 103A.

lessons.title: Soft Wheels, Hard Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: Soft wheels squash to grip and smooth rough ground; hard wheels keep their shape to roll fast and slide on smooth surfaces.
reading: Every wheel flattens a little where it touches the ground. That flat spot is the *contact patch*. A soft wheel flattens more, so its contact patch is larger. A larger patch gives more grip in turns and spreads small bumps over a wider area, so the rider feels less shaking. A hard wheel flattens less. Its small patch grips less and lets the wheel slide more easily.

Squashing a wheel takes energy, and the urethane does not give all of it back as it springs into shape. The lost part turns into a little heat. This loss is called *hysteresis*. On smooth concrete, a soft wheel keeps squashing and recovering with every turn, so it loses more energy than a hard wheel. That is one reason hard wheels feel faster at a skatepark. On rough ground the picture flips: a hard wheel bounces off every pebble while a soft wheel rolls over them.

Hard wheels are also chosen for slides. In a powerslide, the skater turns the board sideways and skids the wheels to slow down. A hard wheel breaks loose smoothly and slides. A soft wheel grips so well that it can stop suddenly and throw the rider forward. On a ledge or a smooth park, skaters who want to slide or land a sideways trick often pick wheels in the high 90s.

Grip and speed pull against each other. A commuter on old sidewalks values a quiet, smooth ride, so a soft wheel wins. A park skater values speed and slides on smooth ground, so a hard wheel wins. Many skaters who ride both pick something in the middle, around 90A to 95A, and accept a little of each problem.

words.d: the small flattened area where a wheel touches the ground
energy lost as heat when a material squashes and springs back
turning the board sideways and skidding the wheels to slow down

look.title: Two Wheels on Two Grounds
look.text: Picture a soft 80A wheel and a hard 99A wheel. First they roll across rough, pebbly asphalt. The soft wheel wraps over each pebble, and the board hums along. The hard wheel jolts on each one, and the rider's feet buzz. Then they roll across smooth park concrete. Now the hard wheel coasts farther, and the soft wheel slows sooner.
look.prompt: Explain why the winner changes when the ground changes, using the words contact patch and hysteresis.

check.q: Why does a soft wheel grip better?
choices: it flattens more and has a larger contact patch
it is made of rubber instead of urethane
check.why: A soft wheel flattens more where it touches the ground, giving a larger contact patch and more grip.

check.q: What is hysteresis in a wheel?
choices: the wheel's color fading in sunlight
energy lost as heat when the urethane squashes and springs back
check.why: Hysteresis is energy lost as heat each time the material deforms and recovers.

check.q: A skater wants to do powerslides at a smooth park. Which wheel fits best?
check.why: A hard wheel breaks loose and slides smoothly; soft wheels grip and can stop suddenly.

lessons.title: Wheel Size
lessons.mainIdea: Bigger wheels roll over cracks and hold speed; smaller wheels are lighter and lower, which helps flip tricks.
reading: Wheel diameter is measured in millimeters across the wheel. Many street wheels are about 50 to 54 millimeters. Many park and transition wheels are about 54 to 60. Cruiser wheels are often 60 millimeters or larger. A larger wheel meets a crack at a gentler angle, so the crack is less likely to stop it. That is why cruisers and longboards use big wheels.

Smaller wheels have their own strengths. They weigh less, so the whole board is lighter to pop and flip. They also sit the deck closer to the ground, which some street skaters like for flip tricks and ledges. A larger wheel carries its momentum longer, which helps on a big bowl but adds weight to every ollie.

Large wheels bring one problem. In a sharp turn the deck tilts toward the wheel. If the wheel is big and the trucks are loose, the wheel can touch the bottom of the deck. This is *wheel bite*. It stops the wheel instantly and can throw the rider. Builders prevent it by tightening the trucks a little, choosing a smaller wheel or adding a *riser pad*, a thin plastic spacer between the truck and the deck.

Diameter also sets how fast the wheel must spin. One turn of a wheel rolls the board one circumference forward, which is π times the diameter. A 54 mm wheel has a circumference of π × 0.054 m = 0.170 m. At 5 meters per second, about a fast jog, it turns 5 ÷ 0.170 = 29.4 times every second. That is about 1,760 turns per minute, which is why bearings matter.

words.d: the distance straight across a wheel through its center, measured in millimeters
when a wheel touches the bottom of the deck in a turn and stops suddenly
a thin spacer between the truck and the deck that lifts the deck higher

look.title: How Fast Wheels Spin at 5 m/s
look.cite: Worked example: turns per second = 5 m/s ÷ (π × diameter)
look.prompt: Why does the smallest wheel spin the most times each second at the same speed?

check.q: Why do cruiser boards often use large wheels?
choices: large wheels roll over cracks more easily
large wheels make flip tricks easier
check.why: A bigger wheel meets a crack at a gentler angle, so it rolls over instead of stopping.

check.q: What is wheel bite?
choices: a wheel touching the deck in a turn and stopping
a wheel cracking from hard landings
wheels wearing into a cone shape
a bearing rusting inside the wheel
check.why: Wheel bite happens when the deck tilts in a turn and its underside touches the wheel, stopping it.

check.q: A 54 mm wheel has a circumference of 0.170 m. How many turns per second does it make at 3.4 m/s?
check.why: Turns per second = speed ÷ circumference = 3.4 ÷ 0.170 = 20.

lessons.title: What Urethane Is
lessons.mainIdea: Urethane wheels are cast from two liquids that react into a tough, elastic plastic, and changing the recipe changes the hardness.
reading: In the early 1960s many skateboards rolled on steel wheels or on clay composite wheels borrowed from roller skates. Steel wheels skidded on small stones and shook the rider. Clay wheels wore quickly and grabbed poorly. In the early 1970s Frank Nasworthy began selling urethane wheels under the name Cadillac Wheels. The new wheels gripped and rolled smoothly, and they helped start skateboarding's second boom.

*Polyurethane*, usually shortened to urethane, is a *polymer*. A polymer is a material made of very long chain molecules built from many small repeating pieces. To make a wheel, a factory mixes two liquids. One is called a polyol and the other an isocyanate. When they meet, they react and link into long chains that also tie to one another. The liquid becomes a solid that is tough and springy.

Wheels are usually *cast*. The mixed liquid is poured into a mold around a core or hub, then cured with time and heat until it hardens. After curing, the wheel is trimmed and its riding surface is cut smooth on a lathe. The chemist can change the hardness by changing the mix. More tightly linked chains give a harder wheel. Looser chains give a softer, more elastic one.

Urethane suits wheels because it resists scraping and tearing better than rubber and stays springy over a wide range of temperatures. It wears slowly, but it does wear. A wheel used for many powerslides can develop a flat spot, a worn patch that makes the wheel thump on every turn. Rotating wheels to new positions helps them wear more evenly.

words.d: a tough, springy plastic used for skate wheels; often called urethane
a material made of very long chain molecules built from small repeating pieces
made by pouring a liquid into a mold and letting it harden

look.title: From Two Liquids to One Wheel
look.text: Step 1: Measure two liquids, a polyol and an isocyanate. Step 2: Mix them, and the chains start to link. Step 3: Pour the mix into a wheel-shaped mold around a core. Step 4: Cure it with time and heat until it is solid. Step 5: Trim it and cut the riding surface smooth on a lathe.
look.prompt: At which step would a maker change something to get a harder wheel, and what would they change?

check.q: Who began selling urethane skateboard wheels as Cadillac Wheels in the early 1970s?
check.why: Frank Nasworthy's Cadillac Wheels brought urethane to skateboarding in the early 1970s.

check.q: What is a polymer?
choices: a kind of wood glue only
a material of very long chain molecules
check.why: A polymer is made of very long chain molecules built from many small repeating pieces.

check.q: How can a chemist make a urethane wheel harder?
choices: change the mix so the chains link more tightly
check.why: Changing the recipe so the chains are more tightly linked gives a harder wheel.

lessons.title: How a Ball Bearing Works
lessons.mainIdea: Bearings replace sliding with rolling, so a wheel spins on its axle with very little friction.
reading: A skateboard wheel turns around a steel axle that does not move. If the wheel's hole simply rubbed on the axle, sliding friction would slow it and wear both parts. A *bearing* fixes this. A skateboard bearing is a ring of small steel or ceramic balls held between two steel rings, called races. The inner race sits on the axle and stays still. The outer race presses into the wheel and turns with it.

The balls roll instead of slide. Rolling friction is far smaller than sliding friction. For example, two dry steel parts sliding on each other might have a friction coefficient around 0.5, while a well-made ball bearing acts more like 0.001 to 0.005. A thin film of grease or oil, called *lubricant*, lowers it further and keeps the metal from wearing. A cage holds the balls evenly spaced so they do not rub against each other.

Almost every skateboard uses the same bearing size, called the 608. It has an 8 millimeter hole, a 22 millimeter outside diameter and a 7 millimeter width. Each wheel takes two bearings, one pressed into each side, so a board has eight. A small metal tube called a spacer can sit between the two bearings inside the wheel so that tightening the axle nut does not squeeze them sideways.

*Shields* cover the sides of the bearing to keep out dirt and water. Some are thin metal; others are rubber seals that block more grit but add a little drag. Dirt is a bearing's worst enemy. One grain of sand between a ball and a race acts like a speed bump on every turn.

words.d: a ring of balls between two races that lets a wheel spin on an axle with little friction
grease or oil that lowers friction and wear between moving parts
covers on the sides of a bearing that keep dirt and water out

look.title: The Standard 608 Skate Bearing
look.prompt: Why does it help skaters that nearly every wheel uses this same size?

check.q: In a skateboard bearing, which part turns with the wheel?
check.why: The outer race is pressed into the wheel and turns with it; the inner race sits still on the axle.

check.q: How many bearings does a full skateboard usually have?
check.why: Each of the four wheels holds two bearings, so a board has eight.

check.q: Why do bearings lower friction?
choices: the balls roll instead of slide
they push the wheel away from the ground
check.why: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, and the balls roll between the races.

lessons.title: ABEC Is Precision, Not Speed
lessons.mainIdea: The ABEC scale rates how precisely a bearing is made, not how fast a skateboard will roll.
reading: Bearing boxes often print a big number: ABEC 3, ABEC 5, ABEC 7. Many buyers think a higher number means a faster board. It does not. *ABEC* stands for the Annular Bearing Engineering Committee, part of the American Bearing Manufacturers Association. Its scale uses odd numbers, 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Each step sets a tighter *tolerance*.

A tolerance is how far a real part may differ from its design size. If a bearing's hole is designed to be 8 millimeters, a tolerance says how much bigger or smaller it may be and still pass. A higher ABEC grade allows smaller errors in the hole, the outside diameter and how true the rings run. Those tight tolerances matter in machines that spin thousands of times a minute for hours, such as precision tools.

The ABEC scale does not rate the things that matter most on a skateboard. It says nothing about the steel's toughness, the quality of the balls, the lubricant, the shields or how the bearing handles side loads. A skateboard bearing takes hard sideways hits on every landing and every turn, which precision machines rarely feel. A well-made bearing with a low ABEC number can roll as well as or better than a poorly made one with a high number.

A board's speed comes mostly from the rider's push and the hill, the wheels and the ground, and how clean the bearings are. A clean, lightly lubricated ABEC 3 bearing will outroll a dirty ABEC 9. Some skate companies skip ABEC ratings and test bearings in their own ways for skateboard loads.

words.d: a scale from the Annular Bearing Engineering Committee that rates how precisely a bearing is made
how far a real part may differ from its design size and still pass
how closely a made part matches its design size and shape

look.title: What the ABEC Grades Cover
look.text: The ABEC classes, 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, set limits on a bearing's dimensions and running accuracy, such as bore size, outside diameter and how true the rings turn. Higher classes have tighter limits.
look.cite: American Bearing Manufacturers Association, ABMA Standard 20, tolerance classes for radial ball bearings
look.prompt: Find one thing a skater cares about that this description does not mention.

check.q: What does a higher ABEC number mean?
choices: the bearing is made to tighter tolerances
check.why: ABEC grades set tolerances; higher numbers mean smaller allowed errors in size and running accuracy.

check.q: Which is NOT rated by the ABEC scale?
choices: how well the bearing handles side loads
check.why: ABEC covers dimensions and running accuracy, not side loads, materials, lubricant or shields.

check.q: Which bearing will most likely roll better on a skateboard?
check.why: Cleanliness and lubrication matter more for rolling than the ABEC grade.

lessons.title: Keeping Bearings Rolling
lessons.mainIdea: Bearings roll best when they are clean, lightly lubricated and not squeezed by an overtightened axle nut.
reading: The axle nut holds the wheel on the truck. If it is too loose, the wheel wobbles and rattles. If it is too tight, it squeezes the bearings sideways and the wheel slows down. First, tighten the nut until it touches the speed washer. Next, back it off a small amount. Then spin the wheel. It should turn freely with only a tiny side-to-side play. Built-in spacers or speed rings help hold this setting.

Water and grit cause most bearing trouble. Riding through puddles can rust the races and balls. Rust makes a gritty, grinding sound and a wheel that stops quickly when spun. If a board gets wet, dry it and spin the wheels before storing it. A bearing that grinds even when clean is worn and should be replaced. Bearings are inexpensive compared with an injury from a wheel that locks up.

To clean bearings, a skater removes the wheels, pries or presses the bearings out with a bearing tool or the truck axle, and gently removes the shields if the design allows. They wash out old grease and dirt with a cleaner the bearing maker recommends, dry the bearings completely and add a few drops of skate lubricant. Too much lubricant attracts more dirt. Working at a table with a towel catches tiny parts and keeps the balls out of the carpet.

Skaters can test a bearing with a spin. Hold the board upside down and flick a wheel. A healthy bearing spins smoothly and quietly and slows gradually. A wheel that stops in a second or two, grinds or wobbles is telling you something. Checking the axle nuts and spins before a session is a fast safety habit.

words.d: the nut that holds the wheel on the truck's axle
a thin metal ring between the bearing and the axle nut or truck
damage to steel caused by water and air, which makes bearings grind

look.title: Setting the Axle Nut
look.text: Picture an upside-down board. You thread the nut onto the axle until it just touches the washer. You give the wheel a flick, and it barely turns: too tight. You back the nut off a small turn. Now the wheel spins and slows smoothly, with a tiny bit of side-to-side play you can feel with your fingers.
look.prompt: What would you feel and hear if the nut were too loose instead?

check.q: What happens if the axle nut is tightened too much?
choices: the bearings are squeezed sideways and the wheel slows
check.why: An overtightened nut presses the bearings sideways, adding friction.

check.q: Why should a skater avoid adding too much lubricant?
check.why: Extra lubricant collects dirt, which slows the bearing.

check.q: A wheel grinds and stops quickly even after cleaning. What is the best choice?
check.why: A bearing that still grinds when clean is worn and should be replaced.

lessons.title: No Part Is Best at Everything
lessons.mainIdea: Every skateboard part trades one strength for another, so engineers start from where and how the board will be ridden.
reading: Engineers call the conditions a design must meet its *requirements*. A park board must survive hard landings and roll fast on smooth concrete. A commuter board must glide over cracks and stay quiet. A street board must be light enough to flip. The limits they cannot change, like cost, weight or the size of a rider's foot, are *constraints*. The best design is the one that fits the job.

Each choice gains something and gives something up. This is a *trade-off*. A thicker deck is stiffer and stronger but heavier. A wider deck is steadier but harder to flip. A soft wheel grips and smooths rough ground but feels slower on smooth concrete. A big wheel rolls over cracks but adds weight and risks wheel bite. Rubber seals keep out grit but add a little drag.

Here is a worked example. A deck goes from seven plies to eight, so it becomes 8 ÷ 7 = 1.14 times as thick, about 14 percent thicker. Its stiffness rises by 1.14 × 1.14 × 1.14 = 1.49, about 49 percent. Its weight also rises by about 14 percent. A maker deciding whether that trade is worth it would ask who rides the board. A heavy rider on big ramps might want the stiffness. A street skater flipping the board all day might not.

Good engineering also tests the guesses. A maker can bend sample decks with a known weight and measure how far they sag, drop them onto concrete again and again, or ride them for weeks and look for cracks. Results lead to changes, and the changes are tested again. This loop of design, test and improve is how boards changed from planks in the 1960s to the shaped laminates of today.

words.d: the conditions a design must meet to do its job
limits a design cannot change, such as cost, weight or size
a choice that gains one strength by giving up another

look.title: Design Brief
look.text: A community center wants ten boards for beginners who will ride an old outdoor basketball court with a few cracks. Riders range from small kids with a grown-up to adults. The boards must be safe, steady and not too expensive. Think about deck width, wheel hardness, wheel size and bearing shields.
look.prompt: List one choice for each part and the trade-off you accepted with it.

check.q: What is a trade-off in design?
choices: gaining one strength by giving up another
check.why: A trade-off means a choice gains something, like stiffness, while giving up something, like low weight.

check.q: A deck goes from 7 to 8 plies. About how much stiffer does it get?
check.why: Thickness rises by 8 ÷ 7 = 1.14, and stiffness by 1.14 cubed, about 1.49, or 49 percent.

check.q: Which is a constraint rather than a requirement?
choices: the board must survive hard landings
the board must roll over cracks
the board must be easy to flip
the board must cost under a set price
check.why: A price limit is a constraint the design cannot change; the others describe what the board must do.

lessons.title: Matching a Setup to the Ground
lessons.mainIdea: A good setup matches deck, wheels and bearings to the ground and the kind of riding the skater plans to do.
reading: Start with the ground. Smooth skatepark concrete or wood ramps reward hard wheels, around 95A to 101A, because they keep their speed and slide when needed. Rough streets, old sidewalks and outdoor courts reward softer wheels, around 78A to 90A, because they absorb bumps and grip. A skater who rides both can split the difference in the low 90s.

Next, pick a size. Street and flat-ground tricks favor smaller wheels, about 50 to 54 millimeters, and a deck that fits the feet without extra weight. Bowls and ramps favor slightly bigger wheels, about 54 to 60 millimeters, and often a wider deck for steady landings at speed. A cruiser for getting around may use wheels of 60 millimeters or more, with riser pads to prevent wheel bite.

Then think about the rider. A tall rider with large feet may want a wider deck so the toes and heels do not hang far over the rails. A beginner often feels safer on a wider, steadier board with medium wheels. Comfort and confidence help a learner practice more, and practice matters more than any part.

Safety comes with every setup. Before riding, check that the axle nuts are on, the wheels spin freely and the trucks are tight enough to stop wheel bite. Then put on a helmet that fits and is buckled, plus wrist guards and pads while learning. A board tuned for the ground is easier to control, and control is what keeps a session safe.

words.d: the combination of deck, trucks, wheels and bearings on one board
a board built for riding around town, usually with large soft wheels
the curved part of a ramp or bowl between the flat ground and the wall

look.title: Three Riders, Three Boards
look.text: Rider one skates a smooth concrete bowl. Rider two rides to school on cracked sidewalks. Rider three practices flip tricks in a flat, smooth parking area at the skatepark. Each needs a different setup, even though all three boards might look alike from across the street.
look.prompt: Choose a wheel hardness and size for each rider and give a reason for each choice.

check.q: Which wheels fit a rider who skates a smooth concrete bowl?
check.why: Hard wheels keep their speed and slide well on smooth concrete.

check.q: Why might a cruiser board need riser pads?
choices: to prevent wheel bite with large wheels
check.why: Large wheels can touch the deck in turns; riser pads lift the deck to prevent wheel bite.

check.q: What should a skater check on the board before riding?
choices: the color of the grip tape
that axle nuts are on and wheels spin freely
the ABEC number on the box
check.why: Checking the axle nuts, wheel spin and truck tightness catches problems before they cause a fall.

review.q: How many plies of maple do most skateboard decks use?
review.why: Most decks are made of seven thin plies of hard maple.

review.q: What does concave add to a deck?
choices: stiffness and edges for the feet
review.why: The side-to-side curve raises stiffness and gives the feet rails to press against.

review.q: Which wheel hardness best fits rough, cracked sidewalks?
review.why: Soft wheels around 80A absorb bumps and grip on rough ground.

choices: hardness, by pressing a pin into a material
review.why: A durometer measures hardness by how far a spring-loaded pin sinks into the surface.

review.q: What does the ABEC scale rate?
choices: how precisely a bearing is made
how many plies a deck has
review.why: ABEC classes set tolerances for a bearing's size and running accuracy, not speed.

review.q: What are urethane wheels made from?
choices: two liquids that react into a tough, springy polymer
review.why: Urethane wheels are cast from a polyol and an isocyanate that link into long chains.

review.q: A 60 mm wheel has a circumference of 0.188 m. About how many turns per second does it make at 5 m/s?
review.why: Turns per second = 5 ÷ 0.188 = about 26.6, so about 27.

review.q: Why do hard wheels often feel faster on smooth park concrete?
choices: they lose less energy to hysteresis because they squash less
review.why: A hard wheel deforms less, so it loses less energy as heat with every turn on smooth ground.
